title: Three Dictionaries in One UMAP
takeaway: The families the authors found by reading text — base64 features, Arabic script features — are also families in geometry: their dictionary vectors point in similar directions. Embedding three dictionaries of different sizes together shows the coarse features from the small run sitting among the finer features that the larger runs split them into.
walkthrough:
Every dot is a direction, not an activation. Each feature learned by a [[sparse-autoencoder]] owns one column of the decoder matrix $W_d$: the [[feature-direction]] it writes into the 512-dimensional space of MLP activations whenever it fires ([[dictionary-decoder]]). Those 512-number columns are the points plotted here. How often a feature fires, and how strongly, plays no part.

[[umap]] squeezes those 512 dimensions down to two, trying to keep points that were neighbours in the original space as neighbours on the page. Neighbourhood is measured by cosine, so this is a picture of *angles* between dictionary vectors — the only comparison that carries information, since the columns are held at unit norm ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]). Settings: `n_neighbors=15`, `min_dist=0.01`.

Read the axes as nothing at all. They have no units, no labels and no fixed orientation. Only co-location means something, and even the gaps between far-apart blobs are not to scale.

Colour is the [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Grey, drawn large, is A/0 with 512 features; dark green is A/1 with 4,096; small light green is A/2 with 16,384. Same transformer, same sparsity coefficient — only dictionary width changes, so grey marks the coarse view and light green the fine one ([[expansion-factor]]).

Because all three share one embedding, each big grey marker tends to sit as a halo beneath a knot of green. That is the geometric shadow of [[feature-splitting]]: one coarse feature and the several finer ones that cover roughly its territory land in the same neighbourhood.

Two knots are named. The [[arabic-script-feature]] family sits in the upper cluster; an arrow points to a small isolated island for the [[base64-feature]] family. Those groups were identified by reading activating text, not by geometry, so their showing up as tight clusters is the figure's one claim ([[feature-geometry-clusters]]).

At the right, set apart from everything, sit the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] features — active on fewer than one token in a million — and the [[dead-neurons]] that never fire. The paper reads these as artifacts of autoencoder training rather than facts about the transformer, and excludes them elsewhere.

One caution the figure itself cannot settle: UMAP will draw clusters out of most inputs, so the picture corroborates the text-based families rather than independently proving them.

terms.definition: The unit vector in the transformer's 512-dimensional MLP activation space that a single learned feature adds when it is active. Here one dot equals one such vector, taken as a column of the autoencoder's decoder matrix.
The output weight matrix of the sparse autoencoder, mapping feature activations back to MLP activations. Its columns are the dictionary directions being embedded in this plot.

A dimensionality reduction method that lays high-dimensional points on a plane while trying to preserve which points were near neighbours. It is what turns each 512-number direction into one $(x,y)$ dot here.
This paper's use of UMAP on feature directions rather than on activations, so that the shape of a dictionary can be browsed. Two such embeddings exist in the paper; this is the second one.

The distance UMAP was told to use: nearness means a small angle between two dictionary vectors, ignoring their length. Length carries no information because decoder columns are constrained to unit norm.
A UMAP setting for how many nearest points define each point's local neighbourhood; larger values emphasise global structure over local. Set to 15 for this plot.

A UMAP setting for the minimum spacing allowed between points in the output plane; smaller values let clumps pack tighter. Set to 0.01 here, tighter than the 0.05 used in the paper's other feature UMAP.
The dictionary learning run on transformer A with 512 learned features — the same count as the MLP has neurons. Its features are the grey, deliberately oversized markers.
The 4,096-feature run on transformer A, the one the paper analyses in most detail. Its features are the solid dark green dots.
The 16,384-feature run on transformer A, the finest of the three shown. Its features are the small light green dots.

The one-layer transformer whose MLP activations all three dictionaries were fit to. A second transformer "B", identical but for its random seed, is used elsewhere for universality checks and does not appear here.
One hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder, treated as a candidate interpretable direction in the model's activation space. The legend counts are the widths of the three autoencoders.

The labelled cluster of features that fire on text written in Arabic script, found by reading activating dataset examples. Their appearance as one tight knot is part of what the figure is meant to show.
The labelled cluster of features that fire inside base64-encoded strings. A/0 has one such feature, A/1 three, A/2 many more.

Features active on fewer than about one dataset example in a million, which the paper says are almost never interpretable and treats as an artifact of autoencoder training. They form their own region on the right of the plot.
Autoencoder hidden units that fire on none of the checked dataset examples at all. Their decoder columns still exist and so still get plotted, landing away from the interpretable mass.

The observation that widening the dictionary turns one feature into a family of more specific ones covering roughly the same territory. In this figure it appears as grey coarse markers sitting under knots of finer green points.
The ratio of autoencoder width to the 512 MLP neurons, i.e. how many more features than neurons the dictionary has. The three runs shown are 1x, 8x and 32x.

The hypothesis that the MLP represents more features than it has neurons by giving each a direction, with the directions not mutually orthogonal. It is why more than 512 directions can be plotted in a 512-dimensional space at all.
The claim this figure supports: conceptually similar features have small angles between their dictionary vectors, so qualitative families are also geometric ones.

The two UMAP output coordinates. They have no units, no fixed orientation and no interpretation; only which points sit together is meaningful, and even inter-cluster distances should not be read quantitatively.

numbers.meaning: Two things at once: the number of neurons in the transformer's MLP layer, and therefore the length of every vector being embedded; and the number of features in run A/0, which is 1x expansion because the dictionary is exactly as wide as the layer.
The width of run A/1, an 8x expansion over 512 neurons. This is the dictionary the paper studies in most detail elsewhere.
The width of run A/2, a 32x expansion. It contributes the most points and, being the finest dictionary, the most split features.
The total number of dots, if the three legend counts are added: 512 + 4,096 + 16,384. The paper does not state this figure; it follows from the legend.
The expansion factors of A/0, A/1 and A/2 relative to the 512 neurons. The paper's full sweep runs from 1x up to 256x (131,072 features); only these three are plotted.
The number of output dimensions of the UMAP. Two is chosen so the result can be printed, not because two dimensions are enough to hold the structure.
UMAP's local-neighbourhood size for this embedding. The paper reports it as a setting and offers no tuning story for it.

UMAP's minimum point spacing for this embedding, tighter than the 0.05 used in the paper's A/0-plus-A/1 UMAP. The tighter value packs each cluster more densely, which is why clumps here read as solid blobs.

The count of base64-specific features as the dictionary grows from 512 to 4,096 to 16,384. This is the paper's headline instance of feature splitting, and it is why the base64 knot contains one grey point, a few dark green ones, and a spray of light green.
The number of A/1's 4,096 features that are dead — active on none of 100 million dataset examples. Dead features from A/1 are among the dark green points in the right-hand region.
The number of A/1 features in the ultralow density cluster. Together with the 168 dead ones, that is about 11% of A/1 excluded from the paper's other analyses.
The number of dataset examples over which activity was checked when classifying features as dead. A feature firing on none of them is called dead, though the paper does not claim it could never fire.

The firing-rate threshold below which a feature counts as ultralow density. The paper defines feature density as the fraction of tokens on which a feature is nonzero, so this is a density under $10^{-6}$.

The two modes of a typical feature density histogram: the left mode is the ultralow density cluster, the right the high density cluster. This is the evidence behind treating the right-hand blob here as a separate population rather than as ordinary rare features.
